title: {{NAME}} and the Valley Where Giants Sleep
moral: True courage means stepping into the unknown and trusting the friends who walk beside you.

pages.content:
The valley stretched out beneath {{NAME}}'s boots like a living painting, vast and impossible and humming with ancient breath. Enormous ferns, each one taller than a house, swayed in a warm wind that smelled of earth and something older still. Somewhere deep below, a sound rolled up through the ground like distant thunder, steady and rhythmic, as though the valley itself had a heartbeat.

A small red fox appeared beside him on the ridge, her amber eyes scanning the green enormity below. She was the kind of fox who had seen many strange things, and yet even she went very still at the sight of it. Between the ferns, enormous shadows moved. Slow. Deliberate. Magnificent.

{{NAME}} had read every book about dinosaurs he could find. He had drawn them on every spare piece of paper in his bedroom. But nothing, not a single illustration or museum skeleton, had prepared him for the sound of a real brachiosaurus breathing.

pages.content:
The fox, whose name was Ember, tugged at {{NAME}}'s bootlace with her teeth. She was trying to tell him something, her ears pivoting like small copper sails catching a signal from every direction at once.

{{NAME}} crouched down to her level and that was when he saw it properly: a baby triceratops, no bigger than a large dog, tangled in a web of thick vines only twenty metres down the slope. Its three small horns were barely the length of {{NAME}}'s fingers. Its enormous dark eyes blinked up at him with an expression he recognised instantly. He had worn that same expression on his first day at a new school. Pure, trembling hope.

'Oh,' {{NAME}} breathed. His whole face went soft with surprise and something warmer. 'You're completely stuck, aren't you?'

pages.content:
Getting a baby triceratops untangled is harder than it sounds, especially when the baby triceratops keeps enthusiastically trying to help and making everything considerably worse. {{NAME}} worked the vines with careful fingers while Ember darted around chewing through the thinner strands with her sharp little teeth. The baby, whom {{NAME}} had already decided to call Clover, wriggled and snorted and at one point sneezed so hard that {{NAME}} sat down hard on the wet moss and laughed until his sides ached.

Then came the sound that silenced everything. A deep, resonant call from the valley below, like a horn carved from the earth itself. Clover's head snapped up, neck straining toward the sound. The ground trembled under three sets of feet, each thud coming closer with purpose and speed.

Clover's mother burst through the ferns. She was the size of a small house, her three great horns gleaming, her frill blazing orange and crimson. She stopped. She looked at {{NAME}}. {{NAME}} did not run. He simply finished untangling the last vine, very slowly and very carefully, and stepped back.

pages.content:
The mother triceratops was called Rona, though {{NAME}} would not know that until much later. Right now she was simply enormous and very close, her warm breath washing over him like a tropical gust, smelling of fern and green things.

Clover bounded to her mother's side, stumbling and righting herself, snorting with joy. Rona lowered her great head slowly until one enormous dark eye was level with {{NAME}}'s face. He could see his own reflection in it, very small, very still, very unafraid.

Ember pressed against his ankle. The jungle held its breath. Every fern, every ancient tree, every hidden creature in the undergrowth seemed to lean in and wait.

Then Rona made a sound, low and soft, nothing like the thunderous call from before. It was almost a hum. She touched the tip of her enormous nose to {{NAME}}'s forehead so gently it felt like a feather. Then she turned, nudged Clover ahead of her, and walked back into the green dark of the valley.

pages.content:
Back on the ridge, as the sun sank low and painted the valley in amber and rose, {{NAME}} sat with Ember curled warm against his side. Below them, the enormous shapes of dinosaurs moved between the ferns like ships between islands, peaceful and unhurried, ancient and alive.

Clover appeared once more at the treeline, looked up at the ridge, and gave a single small snort. Then she disappeared back into the green.

{{NAME}} smiled the kind of smile that starts small and keeps growing. He pulled his journal from his pocket and began to draw, trying to capture the exact shade of Rona's frill, the precise way the valley light fell gold through prehistoric leaves.

Ember yawned and rested her chin on his knee. {{NAME}}'s eyes grew heavier with every stroke of his pencil. It had been the most extraordinary day of his life, and the valley below was still full of secrets he hadn't discovered yet. He fell asleep wondering what Clover's favourite game might be.

Goodnight, brave explorer. Sleep well, and dream of everything waiting just beyond the ferns.
